title: Google Analytics
text:
As part of my professional development at Cal Poly Pomona, I have completed introductory Google Analytics exercises and simulated projects to understand how data can inform communication and team decisions. Below are three projects that blend analytics thinking with my multilingual and collaborative skills.

Note: These are academic simulation projects using Google Analytics demo accounts and sample datasets. They demonstrate my ability to interpret basic metrics, ask the right questions, and present insights clearly.




Objective: Analyze how website visitors who speak different languages engage with content, and recommend localization improvements.
Tools Used:
Google Analytics 4 (Demo Account – Google Merchandise Store) • Google Sheets
Process:
1. Filtered traffic by Language dimension (English, Spanish, Arabic)
2. Compared bounce rates, session duration, and conversion rates across the three groups
3. Noted that Spanish and Arabic speakers had higher bounce rates (65% vs. 45% for English)
Key Insight:
Non-English pages lacked full product descriptions and clear calls-to-action.
Recommendation:
- Translate key landing pages into Spanish and Arabic
- Add language selector to homepage header
Outcome (Simulated):
Implementing these changes in a mock A/B test reduced bounce rates by 18% for Spanish speakers and 22% for Arabic speakers.
Skills Demonstrated:
Dimension filtering • Metric comparison • Data-driven localization recommendations • Cross-cultural awareness




Objective: Create a simple dashboard for a 5‑person academic team to track shared project contributions and communication efficiency.
Tools Used:
Google Analytics 4 (Custom event simulation) • Looker Studio (mock data)
Process:
1. Simulated “event tracking” for team actions (document edits, meeting attendance, message responses)
2. Built a Looker Studio dashboard showing individual and team activity over time
3. Shared dashboard with team members to identify participation gaps
Key Insight:
Two team members had low activity during weeks 3–4; one member accounted for 40% of document edits.
Action Taken:
- Rebalanced task assignments
- Scheduled a mid‑project check‑in to address workload concerns
Result:
Team satisfaction improved (post‑survey score: 4.6/5), and final project was submitted on time with all members contributing.
Skills Demonstrated:
Custom event logic • Dashboard creation • Team process improvement • Data communication




Objective: Analyze traffic patterns for a mock student group website (“CPP Multilingual Connection”) and suggest content improvements.
Tools Used:
Google Analytics 4 (Demo property reconfigured for student org simulation) • Google Slides
Process:
1. Reviewed 3 months of simulated traffic data: - Top source: Direct traffic (40%)
- Top landing page: “Events” (35% of entries)
- High exit rate (70%) on “Join Us” page

Identified that users landed on Events but didn’t sign up because the “Join Us” form was too long.

Recommendation:
- Shorten form from 8 fields to 4
- Add a clear “Sign Up Now” button on every event page
Simulated Result:
Form completion rate increased from 12% to 34% in a follow‑up test.
Presentation:
Delivered findings in a 5‑minute bilingual presentation (English + Arabic) to classmates, receiving feedback on clarity and actionability.
Skills Demonstrated:
Traffic source analysis • Landing page optimization • Form analytics • Bilingual presentation

Step 1 had a lot of new things, explained below are few of them;
case_when() – Helps create categories based on conditions. Much cleaner than writing multiple ifelse statements.
across() – Applies the same calculation to many columns at once. Saves time and reduces repetition.
tidyselect helpers – Select columns by patterns like starts_with() or contains(). Useful for large datasets.
These tools make code shorter and easier to read. They show how experienced analysts work efficiently.

4 Qn 4 – Revealjs Presentations
Revealjs offers features different from PowerPoint.
What it can do:

Show content step by step
Add slide transitions
Use custom themes
Embed code and charts directly in slides
Update visuals when data changes

Strengths:

Reproducible – slides come from code
Charts stay connected to data
Good for technical presentations

Weaknesses:

Requires coding knowledge
Takes longer to set up
Less familiar to most people

Good for data science work. PowerPoint is easier for quick presentations.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
6 Qn 6 – Three Functions from Step 6
left_join()
Merges two datasets while keeping all rows from the first table.
Example: left_join(employees, departments, by = "dept_id")
Result: Employee records with department names added.
rowwise()
Lets you calculate across columns within each row.
Example: df %>% rowwise() %>% mutate(avg = mean(c(score1, score2, score3)))
Result: New column with each row’s average.
case_when()
Creates categories based on conditions.
Example: mutate(age_group = case_when(age < 18 ~ "Child", age < 65 ~ "Adult", TRUE ~ "Senior"))
Result: New column classifying each person.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
7 Qn 7 – What I Liked Most
I enjoyed learning how to clean messy data.
Real data is never perfect. Names are unclear. Values are missing. Information is scattered across tables.
Tidyverse tools help fix these problems. mutate() creates new variables. filter() keeps what matters. joins combine datasets.
The pipe (%>%) connects everything in a clear sequence. You can see each step as data moves through the process.
Wrangling isn’t flashy. But without it, analysis fails. Clean data makes everything else possible.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
8 Qn 8 – Challenges and Solutions
Challenge 1 – Too many functions to remember
Some functions do similar things. Easy to mix them up.
Solution: Practice regularly. Use cheat sheets. Review class examples.
Challenge 2 – Debugging errors
Code runs but gives wrong results. Hard to find the problem.
Solution: Run code step by step. Check data after each step. Test with small samples first.
Challenge 3 – Syntax mistakes
Missing parentheses or wrong column names cause failures.
Solution: Read error messages carefully. Check column names. Use RStudio’s highlighting.
Regular practice helps. Each project builds confidence.

title: W08-Data Analytics (Google Cloud BigQuery and Looker Studio)
section: 3 Introduction to the Basics of BigQuery
text:
3 Introduction to the Basics of BigQuery

This course allowed me to gain a good idea of the functionality of BigQuery as a cloud-based data warehouse. I was also able to know how organizations can store and process big data sets without involving the use of traditional database systems. I also examined the underlying data organization as tables and query parameters that help in extracting useful information using publicly available datasets. The experience enabled me to understand the importance of scalable data solutions in contemporary analytics. The speed and other features of BigQuery enabled one to concentrate on insights rather than technical constraints and this is useful in a business world where immediate decisions are necessary.
I also exercised in writing SQL queries to filter, sort and aggregate data. I learned how to utilize functions like COUNT and AVG which have aided me in summarizing massive datasets into valuable information. I also considered joining various tables, which taught me how data provided by one or more sources may be used together to provide solutions to multifaceted queries. The importance of these skills lies in the fact that they are representative of real-world analytics tasks in which data is not always clean or in a central place. In general, I became confident in my ability to use SQL as a means of deriving information out of raw data.


3.1 Creating Data Visualizations in looker Studio

Besides the data analysis, I was taught to present data with the help of Looker Studio. I also linked data sets in BigQuery and performed visualization like line charts to monitor trends in time. This led me to realize how the visual tools ease the complex data and make it more accessible to the wider audience. I learned that data visualization is crucial since they enable parties to perceive patterns effectively and make sound decisions within a short time without the need to have technical expertise.
I also read about other types of charts, such as column and geo charts, and it allowed me to learn how the visualization choices should be considered in terms of their effect on interpretation. I refined the presentation of the data by modifying the measures and dimensions. The practice guided me to clear and simple are major principles in designing dashboards. Raw numbers alone cannot provide as much information as a carefully designed visualization can. This is an important skill in business contexts where clarity of communication determines the strategy and performance.



3.2 Using Data Analytics in Real World Problems

The course has enabled me to use my abilities in applying information of global temperatures in a real world so as to have the context in which the learning will be undertaken. I used a systematic method when going through a process of defining a problem, analyzing data, and presenting a result in a visual form. This exercise has made me realize that data analytics is not a purely technical task; it is a process that requires critical thinking and interpretation, too. It strengthened the theme that whenever dealing with data, it must back up with meaningful questions.
I also got to know how using BigQuery with the help of Looker Studio will provide an entire workflow with analytics. BigQuery is used when it comes to processing data and visualizing and reporting are the tasks that Looker Studio handles. This integration demonstrated to me how the tools were integrated in the real-life situations. Towards the close of the course, I was better equipped to use data analytics in business. I can now interpret raw data to create actionable information that would aid in making a decision.

title: Data Science
text:
My approach to data science emphasizes reproducible research, clean data wrangling, and compelling visualizations using the R and Tidyverse ecosystem.



Exploring the Wooldridge Dataset
Using ggplot2 and wooldridge packages, I analyzed student attendance and GPA data. The project involved: - Crafting professional tables using the gt package. - Comparing Dodge, Stack, and Faceted Barplots to properly evaluate group differences. - Using Boxplots with jitter to understand distribution spreads alongside central tendencies. - Evaluating Moderation effects (e.g. how freshman status moderates the impact of ACT scores on attendance).
View Full Reflection & Code



Tidyverse Workflows
I’ve gained deep experience in structuring and cleaning messy data using Tidyverse: - Extensive use of case_when(), across(), and tidyselect helpers to streamline workflows. - Implementing robust data cleaning pipelines that prioritize quality over quantity. - Merging datasets confidently using join functions like left_join(). - Building automated slide decks and reports directly from code using Quarto and Reveal.js.
View Full Reflection



Scaling Statistical Analysis
- Automating repetitive tasks and transitioning from loops to functional programming using purrr::map(). - Utilizing the broom package to tidy and organize complex model outputs. - Developing reusable processes and functions to handle varied data inputs efficiently.

Applying data analysis to real-world cloud infrastructure: - Query: Writing structured SQL in BigQuery to filter and aggregate large public datasets. - Transform: Cleaning and shaping query results. - Communicate: Designing interactive visual reports and dashboards using Looker Studio to track trends and geographical patterns.

# Recoding/Relabelling the Sophomore Column
df_soph <- df %>%
  mutate(label_soph = factor(soph,

geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.9) +

  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "purple", "Sophomore" = "skyblue")) +
  labs(title = "Final Score by ACT and Sophomore Status (Stacked)",
       x = "ACT Score", y = "Final Score",
       fill = "Sophomore Status") +
  theme_minimal()

title: M03-2: Data Visualization-Application Assignment

text:
4.2 Compare the dodged bar plot from Q3.2 with the dodged bar chart from Q4.2. Which chart would you trust and why?

The dodged bar chart in 3.2 plots every individual final score, creating a crowded field of overlapping bars that obscures rather than illuminates. By displaying raw observations instead of group summaries, it fails to convey clear trends.
Section 4.2 takes a more effective approach, aggregating final scores by ACT level and sophomore status to show average performance. This summary cuts through the noise, revealing central tendencies and enabling direct group comparisons. The result is a clear visualization of how ACT scores, final grades, and the moderating variable relate.
In short, the mean-based chart is the superior choice—it distills the data into a trustworthy, informative summary that supports sound conclusions.

4.3 What would you say about the differences in the patterns of relationships between ACT and final scores shown in the sophomore and non-sophomore groups?
For both freshmen and sophomores, higher ACT scores correspond to higher mean final scores. Yet at most points along the ACT spectrum, sophomores hold a slight edge. This suggests two forces at work: ACT scores capture underlying academic ability, while the sophomore bump likely reflects the benefits of having already navigated a year of college and its academic demands.

title: M03-2: Data Visualization-Application Assignment
section: 5.3 What would you say about the differences in the patterns of relationships between ACT and final scores shown in the sophomore and non-sophomore groups?
text:
5.3 What would you say about the differences in the patterns of relationships between ACT and final scores shown in the sophomore and non-sophomore groups?
Sophomores consistently outperform freshmen on final scores, with slightly higher medians observed across most ACT score levels. This pattern supports the hypothesis that additional academic experience or maturity contributes to better performance.
Both groups show similar interquartile ranges, indicating comparable variability within each class. However, freshmen at the lower end of the ACT distribution display more extreme low outliers, suggesting a greater likelihood of very poor final performance among this subgroup.
The performance gap between sophomores and freshmen remains relatively stable across the ACT score spectrum. This consistency points to a main effect of class status rather than an interaction with ACT scores—the sophomore advantage manifests as a consistent upward shift in the score distribution, with no evidence that the relationship between ACT and final scores differs by group.

6.2 Is the relationship between x and y shown in the non-freshman group (denoted as “0” in the data) the same as that shown in the freshman group?
There is a moderating effect of freshman status on the relationship between ACT scores and attendance. For non-freshmen, there is a pronounced and steady increase in attendance corresponding with higher ACT scores. Conversely, this gradient is shallower and less systematic for freshmen. The data therefore indicate that the influence of ACT scores on attendance is conditional upon freshman status.

text:
7.2 In sum, describe what you found in the relationship between x and y and how the relationship pattern is different across the two freshman status groups.
When exploring moderation, visualize the relationship, not just the means. Scatter plots with fitted lines allow you to assess both slope differences (the interaction) and intercept differences (the main effect). Here, the plot clearly shows that freshmen not only attend less across all ACT levels but also show a diminished response to ACT. This nuanced story would be completely lost in a traditional bar plot of means.

About
I’m a motivated university student currently pursuing a Bachelor’s degree at California State Polytechnic University, Pomona (Cal Poly Pomona). I am passionate about learning, personal growth, and developing professional skills that prepare me for future career opportunities.
I bring strong communication abilities, multilingual fluency, and a commitment to collaboration. title: Projects
text:
Below are selected academic and collaborative projects that demonstrate my commitment to teamwork, multilingual communication, and practical problem-solving.



Role: Team Lead & Translator (Arabic/English)
Course: BUS 3000 – Professional Communication
Timeline: September 2025 – December 2025
Challenge: Many international students on campus struggled to find basic services (health center, tutoring, housing assistance) due to language barriers and fragmented information.
My Role:
- Led a team of 4 students to create a trilingual resource guide (English, Arabic, Spanish)
- Translated all content into Arabic and coordinated with Spanish-speaking teammate
- Presented the guide to the university’s International Student Office for feedback
Result:
- Guide distributed to 150+ students during orientation week
- Received positive feedback from international student advisors
- Project earned an A grade and was recommended for wider university use
Skills Demonstrated:
Multilingual translation • Team leadership • Cross-cultural communication • Project coordination




Role: Facilitator & Note-taker
Course: MHR 3010 – Organizational Behavior
Timeline: February 2026 – April 2026
Challenge: A 5-member team had to solve a complex business simulation involving resource allocation, deadline pressure, and conflicting viewpoints among members.
My Role:
- Acted as primary facilitator, ensuring all voices were heard
- Documented decisions and action items in shared Google Docs
- Mediated a disagreement between two members by proposing a compromise based on data from the simulation
Result:
- Team completed simulation two days ahead of deadline
- Earned 95% on the final report
- Peer feedback praised my ability to “keep everyone focused and respected”
Skills Demonstrated:
Conflict mediation • Meeting facilitation • Documentation • Adaptability under pressure




Role: Panelist & Co-Organizer
Type: Community Service / Leadership
Timeline: March 2026
Challenge: Current high school students needed relatable, multilingual advice about transitioning to a four-year university, especially from first-generation backgrounds.
My Role:
- Co-organized a panel of 6 alumni now at Cal Poly Pomona, UC Riverside, and Chaffey College
- Shared personal journey from high school to university, emphasizing study habits and resource use
- Answered questions in English and Spanish for bilingual attendees
Result:
- 40+ high school students attended
- Post-event survey showed 92% felt more confident about applying to college
- Invited back for fall 2026 session
Skills Demonstrated:
Public speaking (bilingual) • Event coordination • Mentorship • Community engagement
